L.                    maidenhair fern (Latin marginal gloss)

CAUCALIS

Some call it caucon, or wild daucon; others call it [...]tis; Democritus calls it bryss[on]; the Romans call it pede gallinaceum; others call it pede pulli; the Egyptians call it seseli. It has a stem about a span high, or even taller, somewhat hairy, with leaves resembling celery; at the top it bears fine, hairy, fennel-like divisions, and a white, fragrant umbel-flower. This too is eaten as a vegetable, both cooked and raw. It is also diuretic when taken fresh.

CALLITRICHON

Some call it polytrichon; others trichomanes; others adianton; others xenopteron; others pteris; others pteron; others arsion; others call the plant korion. The Egyptians call it egyer, the Romans call it cincinalis; others call it tinula; others terra capillus [earth-hair]; others super tiaoum terra. [...] Its leaves resemble coriander, [...] black, strong, [...] lacking stalk. It bears neither stalk nor flower; its root is useless. But the herb itself, when drunk, can help with asthma, jaundice, and difficulty urinating; it also breaks up stones, settles the bowels, helps those bitten by dogs, and helps with discharge from the stomach. It also helps bring on menstruation and stops [bleeding], and it checks the coughing up of blood. When swallowed, it also helps against venomous bites and against alopecia (hair loss), by causing hair to grow thickly; it clears away scrofulous swellings and abscesses, [...] and mixed with myrtle [...] when fumigated and applied to the head, it makes a woman's hair grow thicker. It also makes amber-colored... and makes quails more combative when mixed into their feed. It grows in shaded, damp places, by walls, and near springs.

Kyndam, or Kynokrambe: Kynokephalion (Dog's-head plant)

Some call it wild Linozostis... [illegible]
...having taken the foam...
It sends up a tender stem about a span high,
whitish, bearing leaves
like Linozostis or ivy, somewhat whitish,
set at intervals; it bears
a small round fruit
lying beside the leaves.

The stem and leaves, when drunk, have the
power to move the bowels; or when eaten as a vegetable
and boiled, the water
draws off bile and watery matter.

Some call it Antirrhinon, some Areinon,
some Boukraston, some Kourion,
some Pithekion, some Kynorodon,
some wild Lychnis, the prophets call it Alkim-,
some Kyriomorphon, some Neotheos;
the Egyptians call it Aisou, some Ormenisph-,
some Katakirsai; the Romans call it Tigaloussaba,
some Tragatigilloi, some Herba
Asinina, some Veneriam.
It grows abundantly with thin leaves,
and on its stem the flowers are white or
purplish-yellow and handsome, which is why
it is also called wild Lychnis.
It bears fruit resembling that of the chaste-tree (vitex).
It is said that this plant is antipathetic,
and when worn as an amulet against drugs, it also
confers charm when applied as an ointment, altogether.
